Characteristics table:

- Accuracy class: (Ⅲ)
- Fraction of mpe, pi: 0.0
- Excitation voltage: DC15V, ≤400mA → excitation_voltage: 15 V (DC), excitation_voltage_max_current: 400 mA
- Maximum number of verification scale intervals, n: ≤ 6000 → {min: null, max: 6000}
- Temperature range: -10℃~+40℃ → {min: -10, max: 40}, °C
- Power supply: AC:100 V~240 V, 50Hz; DC or rechargeable battery: 12V →
  - power_supply_voltage (AC): {min: 100, max: 240} V
  - power_supply_frequency: 50 Hz
  - power_supply_voltage (DC/battery): 12 V
  - power_supply_type: "AC" / "DC or rechargeable battery"
- Software version: V20XXX with note

Model family: DZ2008-D1 series with models DZ2008-D1-F and DZ2008-D1-M. All characteristics are shared (colspan=2), so model_level entries would be redundant but the matrix detection rule says varying attributes go in model_level. Since all attributes are the same for both models, I can keep them at type_level. But it might be good to populate model_family.models with the two variants.

Actually, let me consider: the table shows Type DZ2008-D1 covering two variants DZ2008-D1-F and DZ2008-D1-M. All other characteristics are common (colspan 2). So type_level for all characteristics, and model_family with two models.

For the power supply, there are two lines: AC and DC/battery. I could model this as config_level with axis "power_supply_type":
- attribute: power_supply_voltage, axis: power_supply_type, values: [{condition: "AC", value: {min:100, max:240}, unit_symbol: "V"}, {condition: "DC or rechargeable battery", value: 12, unit_symbol: "V"}]
- attribute: power_supply_frequency, values: [{condition: "AC", value: 50, unit_symbol: "Hz"}]

That seems reasonable per rule 5 for configuration variation. Or simpler: two separate type_level attributes like power_supply_voltage_ac and power_supply_voltage_dc. Both approaches work. I'll use config_level since it's cleaner per the schema.

Actually, let me think. Rule 3 example: `110-240V AC 50/60Hz` → power_supply_voltage {min:110, max:240} V, power_supply_frequency {min:50,max:60} Hz, power_supply_type "AC". Here we have two supply types. I'll use config_level for voltage with axis power_supply_type, and type_level for frequency (only applies to AC). Hmm, frequency under AC only. I could put frequency in config_level too with condition "AC".

Excitation voltage: DC15V, ≤400mA:
- excitation_voltage: value 15, unit_symbol "V", type... Actually DC15V means DC 15 V. Could add excitation_voltage_type: "DC".
- excitation_current_max: {min: null, max: 0.4} A or 400 mA. The markdown says ≤400mA. So value {min: null, max: 400}, unit "mA". I'll use unit_symbol "mA" raw.

Software version: V20XXX — value string "V20XXX". Footnote-like note explaining V20 vs XXX. I'll add the note as a footnote? It's not marked with a footnote marker; it's inline "note:". I could include it in description or as a footnote with marker... The rules say footnotes are extracted definitions like "1) ...". This note has no marker. I could add it to the certificate description or a footnote with no marker. Safer: include software_version as type_level with value "V20XXX" and maybe include the note text in a footnote entry? Fabricating a marker would be wrong. I'll add the note text to the value's... hmm. Maybe I can include a "software_version_note" attribute with the string. Or just include the note in footnotes with marker null? The schema says footnotes[]: marker, text. I could do {marker: null, text: "V20 refers to the legally relevant part..."}. That seems acceptable — the schema allows marker to be null presumably. Actually rule 7 says extract footnote definitions; this is a note, not a numbered footnote. I'll add it as a footnote with marker null, and not reference it via footnote_markers on the value. Hmm, but that could be misinterpreted. Alternatively, put the whole note as a separate characteristic "software_version_note". I think footnote with null marker is cleaner. Let me do that.

Accuracy class: (Ⅲ) → class III. recommendation.accuracy_classes: ["III"] — Roman numeral Ⅲ is a Unicode char; canonical would be "III". I'll use "III".

Fraction of mpe, pi: 0.0 → p_i. Canonical label: fraction_of_mpe_pi. Value 0.0. Hmm, 0.0? That seems odd for an indicator — typically p_i = 1 for indicators. But the markdown says 0.0. Don't fabricate; record 0.0. Wait — could "0.0" be a misread? Just record as given: 0.

Maximum number of verification scale intervals n: ≤ 6000 → {min: null, max: 6000}, unit_symbol null (dimensionless counts). Canonical label: max_verification_scale_intervals_n.

Temperature range: -10°C to +40°C → {min: -10, max: 40}, °C.

Recommendation object: id "R76", edition 2006, scheme "A", accuracy_classes ["III"].

Certificate: number "R76/2006-A-CN2-26.02", scheme "A", page_total 2, member_state "P. R. China", date_issued "2026-09-03", oiml_issuer_id — not present explicitly. Omit.

Issuing authority: name, address_lines ["No.18, Bei San Huan Dong Lu, Chaoyang Dist., Beijing, P.R.China"] — footer includes "100029, P.R.China". I'll include postal code line too: address_lines: ["No.18, Bei San Huan Dong Lu,", "Chaoyang Dist., Beijing,", "100029, P.R.China"]. Or the header version. Combine: ["No.18, Bei San Huan Dong Lu, Chaoyang Dist., Beijing, 100029, P.R.China"]. I'll use the footer with postal code as separate lines.

model_family: family_name "DZ2008-D1 series", models: [{model_id: "DZ2008-D1-F", label: ...}, {model_id: "DZ2008-D1-M"}]. Should I include "DZ2008-D1" as the base? The table shows Type: DZ2008-D1 with variants -F and -M. Models list should be the variants: F and M.

Characteristics type_level:
- accuracy_class: {value: "III"}? Accuracy class is not numeric; value "Ⅲ" → canonical "III". I'll include accuracy_class: {value: "III", unit_symbol: null, unit_id: null, footnote_markers: []}. Actually maybe accuracy_classes is in recommendation; but type_level attribute also fine. I'll include it.
- fraction_of_mpe_pi: {value: 0.0}
- excitation_voltage: {value: 15, unit_symbol: "V"}
- excitation_voltage_type: {value: "DC"}
- excitation_current_max: {value: {min: null, max: 400}, unit_symbol: "mA"}
- max_verification_scale_intervals_n: {value: {min: null, max: 6000}}
- temperature_range: {value: {min: -10, max: 40}, unit_symbol: "°C"}

Config level:
- attribute power_supply_voltage, axis power_supply_type, values: [{condition "AC", value {min:100,max:240}, unit "V"}, {condition "DC or rechargeable battery", value 12, unit "V"}]
- attribute power_supply_frequency, axis power_supply_type, values: [{condition "AC", value 50, unit "Hz"}]

Wait — schema for config_level values: {condition, value}. Rule 5 says values follow the same structured form: {condition, value, unit_symbol}. So structured objects with condition.

Should I instead flatten to type_level power_supply_voltage_ac etc.? The rule 3 example suggests splitting AC/DC. The config_level approach handles dual supply types elegantly. I'll go with config_level.

Matrix_tables: The characteristics table is not really multi-dimensional beyond variants; all shared. I don't think we need matrix_tables. Skip.

Components: not applicable (indicator itself). Skip.

Footnotes: the software note. {marker: null, text: "V20 refers to the legally relevant part of the software and will not be changed, while XXX refers to the non-legally relevant part of the software and ranges from 000 to 999."}

Date formats: The schema says date_issued; use ISO "2026-09-03".

Let me also double check "Fraction of mpe, pi: 0.0". Hmm, actually for class III indicators, p_i might be... whatever, record as 0.0. Actually wait — maybe it's "1.0"? The markdown says 0.0. Don't fabricate; use 0.0.

Value shape: all values should be structured objects {value, unit_symbol, unit_id, footnote_markers}. Let me make sure each characteristic value has unit_symbol and footnote_markers fields where relevant. The schema example shows {value, unit, footnote_markers[]}. In the layered schema: `<label>: {value, unit, footnote_markers[]}`. Rule 2 shape: {value, unit_symbol, unit_id, footnote_markers}. I'll use unit_symbol and unit_id per rule 2/3.
